Getting started with compfit

compfit.Rmd

You describe a compartmental (SIR-type) ODE model in three small spreadsheets, and compfit fits it, by maximum likelihood or Bayesian sampling. It then helps you analyse the result: posterior summaries, predictive plots, global (Sobol) and local sensitivity, practical identifiability, and reproducible code export. You write down the model; the package handles the ODE build, the loss or likelihood, the solver, and the plots.

This guide walks through that workflow and the sheet grammar it uses. For a worked example that runs live, with real output and figures, see the companion article “Fitting an SIR model with compfit”.

At a glance

The basic workflow is three calls: load, fit, plot.

library(compfit)

# A scenario is a folder of three sheets: model, data, and optional dummy series.
sc <- load_scenario("path/to/MyScenario",
                    combined_file = "dataCombined.csv",
                    dummy_file    = "dataDummy.csv",
                    params_file   = "modelParams.csv")

# Fit by maximum likelihood. backend = "r" runs entirely in R, with no Julia.
fit <- fitCompartmentalModel(sc$modelParams, sc$dataCombined,
                             method = "lbfgsb",
                             solver = solver_control(backend = "r"))
summary(fit)

# Inspect the fit (and any dummy series) as a grid of per-stream panels.
plot_fit(fit, data_dummy = sc$dataDummy)$grid

The rest of this guide covers each step.

Choosing a backend

Solving the ODE, and for Bayesian fits drawing the posterior, can run on any of three backends. Pick one with solver_control(backend = ...):

backend engine needs good for
"julia" (default) Julia OrdinaryDiffEq + Turing NUTS a Julia session fastest solves; gradient-based Bayesian sampling with full feature support
"r" deSolve + gradient-free MCMC (BayesianTools) nothing extra Julia-free fitting; small models, quick checks, teaching
"stan" Stan NUTS via rstan a C++ toolchain gradient-based Bayesian sampling, no Julia; best for censored counts

Maximum-likelihood fits give the same answer on every backend, just faster on Julia. For Bayesian fits the differences matter:

  • "julia" is the main path: fast NUTS, every family and every data-cell type.
  • "r" uses a gradient-free sampler (BayesianTools DEzs), seeded from a quick MLE fit. It is much slower and mixes far worse, so it is best for a small model or a sanity check. For real inference use Julia or Stan.
  • "stan" gives gradient-based NUTS with no Julia. All three backends now score every data-cell type (observed, censored, interval [A,B]/[A,B]~s, asymmetric) and all four families. For censored count data Stan is actually the strongest option (see the CDF note below).

Every data-cell type now works on all three Bayesian backends. The one remaining backend nuance is that Julia cannot score a censored/interval/asymmetric cell on a discrete family (see the CDF note); Stan and R can.

Everything downstream (posterior_report(), plot_prior_posterior(), and so on) works the same whichever backend you pick.

The Julia backend needs a one-time setup per session. The first call also installs the required Julia packages (OrdinaryDiffEq, Turing, Distributions), which takes a few minutes; later calls are quick:

setup_julia()

The bridge also initialises lazily, so setup_julia() mainly just does the slow part up front. The R and Stan backends need no Julia at all.

Choosing the Julia ODE solver

On the Julia backend, solver_control(solver = ...) takes any OrdinaryDiffEq solver, written as the Julia constructor and passed straight through to the solve. The default auto-switches between a non-stiff and a stiff method and is a good fit for almost every compartmental model, so you rarely need to change it. When you do:

solver Kind Use when
"AutoTsit5(Rosenbrock23())" (default) auto-switching general purpose; leave it here unless a fit misbehaves
"Tsit5()" non-stiff plain, fast, smooth dynamics
"Vern7()", "Vern9()" non-stiff, high accuracy tight tolerances
"Rosenbrock23()", "Rodas5()", "Rodas4()" stiff (Rosenbrock) stiff systems (fast/slow rates)
"KenCarp4()", "TRBDF2()" stiff (implicit) larger stiff systems
"AutoVern7(Rodas5())" auto-switching like the default but higher accuracy 
fit <- fitCompartmentalModel(sc$modelParams, sc$dataCombined, method = "lbfgsb",
                             solver = solver_control(solver = "Rodas5()"))

The full menu is in the DifferentialEquations.jl solver guide. This choice is Julia-only: the R backend uses deSolve’s auto-switching lsoda, and the Stan backend uses Stan’s ode_rk45 (or ode_bdf via solver_control(solver = "bdf")).

The scenario sheets

A scenario is one folder holding the input files:

MyScenario/
  modelParams.xlsx    # the model: compartments, parameters, rates, time grid
  dataCombined.xlsx   # the data: one row per observed stream (optional; omit to simulate)
  dataDummy.xlsx      # optional derived series to overlay

load_scenario() reads all three. sc then holds sc$modelParams, sc$dataCombined, sc$dataDummy, and a sc$plot_path for output. Formats .csv, .xlsx, .tsv, .rds, .parquet and more are detected automatically.

sc <- load_scenario(
  "path/to/MyScenario",
  combined_file = "dataCombined.xlsx",
  dummy_file    = "dataDummy.xlsx",
  params_file   = "modelParams.xlsx"
)

modelParams: the model

The model sheet uses column groups:

  • States: the compartments, in order, with their initial values. You can name them freely, S, I, R or X1, X2, X3. The States column sets both the names and the order. Each entry is *name=val (fixed), name=[lo,hi] (fitted), or *name=<expr> (a parameter-dependent initial value, for example *X2=init_inf_0*N0_0).
  • Parameters: *name=val is fixed. A fitted parameter is given by its prior, either the box form name=[lo,hi] (Uniform) or a named distribution (see the priors table below). A Bayesian fit uses the stated distribution as the prior. An MLE fit only needs a search box, so an unbounded prior (a plain Normal, say) is given a finite range from the distribution (mean ± 4 sd, or its natural support). Add a trailing [lo,hi] to set the MLE bounds exactly.
  • Start value (optional): append |value to a box to set the optimiser’s starting point, for example beta=[0,3]|2.5. Without it the search starts at the box midpoint. Use |random (or |rand) instead to draw the start uniformly from the box, for example beta=[0,3]|random; the draw is seeded by optim_control(seed = ), so it is reproducible, and seed = NULL gives a fresh start each run (handy for multi-start / escaping a poor local optimum). This drives the L-BFGS-B start (and the Bayesian MAP warm-start); deoptim and hypercube scan the whole box already, so a single start is moot there.
  • Linear<j> / Quadratic<j>: the first- and second-order rate coefficients, one pair of columns per compartment. A blank cell counts as zero, and so does a whole column you leave out (that compartment simply gets no such terms).
  • Constant (optional): a zeroth-order term added straight to a compartment’s rate, one value per compartment (row i feeds dX[i]). Use it for an inflow that does not depend on any state, such as a constant birth or immigration rate, which cannot be written as a Linear (*X[j]) or Quadratic (*X[i]*X[j]) term. A cell may be a number, a parameter name, an expression of parameters, or a $-prefixed time-function ($1000*exp(-0.1*time)) – the same grammar as a Linear coefficient, minus the *X[j]. A blank cell or an absent column is zero.
  • Others: the time grid, with startpoint, endpoint, partition, and an optional cutoff. The axis is annual (integer years), and by convention the initial state sits at startpoint - 1.
  • Functions (optional): time-varying helpers, for example gamma_t<-gamma*(1+ramp*time).
  • Conditions (optional): constraints turned into a fitting penalty, for example beta>gamma.
  • _Level<j> (optional): which compartments share a mixing population (age, sex, region). The name after _ is up to you (_Level1, _Age1, and so on), and cells take a compartment number or name. Leave it out and all compartments form a single population.

Reserved names. A Bayesian fit uses sigma (the Gaussian or log-normal noise scale) and phi/phi<i> (negbin dispersion) as its own parameters, so a model parameter or state cannot be named sigma or phi. Using one raises a clear error on method = "bayes"; MLE is unaffected. Just rename it, for example an SEIR incubation rate as sigma_ei.

Separately, a handful of names collide with variables the code generator emits and are rejected for any fit (parameters, states, and functions alike): Julia keywords and the solver internals t, p, X, du, dX, parms; the level populations N1, N2, … and their sum total_pop; and the per-term helpers f<ij>, g<ij>, cst<i>, secOrd_<i>_<j>. Also avoid declaring both a quantity and its _0 alias (e.g. beta and beta_0). Note N0 is fine (a common fixed initial-population parameter) – only N1 upward are taken.

The sheet is checked up front by validate_modelParams(), which reports entry mistakes with a message naming the offending column and cell: a non-numeric fixed value, a reversed or non-numeric box [lo,hi], an out-of-range Quadratic target, a typo in a coefficient, or a missing time-grid field. You can call it yourself, or turn off the automatic check with options(compfit.validate = FALSE).

Priors

A fitted parameter or state can take any of these priors, written in the States or Parameters cell:

Prior Sheet syntax Support
Uniform [lo,hi] [lo,hi]
Normal Normal(mu,sd) real line
Log-normal LogNormal(mu,sd) positive
Beta Beta(a,b) (0,1)
Gamma Gamma(a,b) positive
Student-t StudentT(nu,mu,sigma) real line (heavy tails; nu = df)

Every named distribution (all but the bare box) can be truncated by appending a [lo,hi], for example Normal(0.4,0.1)[0,1] or LogNormal(-1,0.5)[0,5]. The SIR_priors and SEIR_priors example scenarios exercise all of them.

dataCombined: the observations

One row per observed stream: a Formula (what the stream measures, for example X2 or rho*X2), an optional Label (its display name, which defaults to the Formula when omitted or blank), an optional Likelihood family, and one column per year.

Weight and Average are optional per-stream scaling columns for the MLE objective, and they do not affect Bayesian fits. Omit them and Weight defaults to 1 while Average is set to 1 / mean(observed) per stream, so streams of different magnitude count comparably. Include either column to override.

Each data cell is parsed as one of:

Cell Meaning
a number observed value (0 is a genuine zero)
x or blank missing / unobserved
<L / <=L left-censored: true value strictly / at-or-below L
>L / >=L right-censored: true value strictly / at-or-above L
[A,B] interval-censored: true value in [A,B], flat within (A < B)
[A,B]~s soft interval: plateau [A,B], exponential shoulders of scale s (~sl,su for asymmetric shoulders)
A->B asymmetric: recorded A, soft toward B (deviation \|B-A\|)
A+ / A- asymmetric: recorded A, soft up/down, deviation from the stream’s Likelihood column

The CDF-based cells (<, <=, >, >=, [A,B], A->B, A+, A-) work for every family on the R backend. On the Julia/NUTS path, though, logcdf is not autodifferentiable for the discrete families, so a censored poisson or negbin cell fails there. You have three options: run that fit on the Stan backend, which uses analytic discrete CDFs and handles censored counts directly (this is the one case where Stan is the strongest backend); put the cell on a continuous (gaussian or lognormal) stream, as in the shipped SIR and SEIR examples; or use the soft interval [A,B]~s, a plain penalty on the model mean (log g(mu), no CDF) that works for every family under NUTS. Discrete streams can always carry plain observed and missing (x) cells on any backend.

The soft interval [A,B]~s says “most plausibly in [A,B], tapering off outside with scale s”. At A - s (or B + s) the penalty is one log-unit. It is the tool for “above 100, but most of the mass in 110–130”: write [110,130]~10. A hard [110,130] would instead forbid everything outside the band.

How censored and interval cells enter each fit. In the MLE (least-squares) loss they become one-sided or two-sided hinge penalties: exactly zero while the model prediction satisfies the bound or sits inside [A,B], then growing quadratically once it strays outside. In the Bayesian fit they are proper censored likelihood terms (P(Y >= L), P(A <= Y <= B) via the CDF), which keep some curvature even inside the region. Note that >L versus >=L only matters for the discrete Bayesian CDF, not for the MLE hinge.

The Likelihood column declares each stream’s family (Bayesian fits only; the MLE loss is least-squares and ignores it). The families:

Family Likelihood value Data Notes
Gaussian gaussian continuous proportional-error Normal; the default when the column is absent
Log-normal lognormal positive
Poisson poisson counts
Negative binomial negbin over-dispersed counts mean–dispersion form, with a fitted dispersion per stream

All four families work on all three backends. Each also has a couple of aliases (normal, lnorm, pois, nbinom, nb), and non-integer data on a count family is rounded, with a warning.

The column can also carry a global deviation for A+/A- cells:

gaussian                  # family only
gaussian; asym=4          # family plus a deviation of 4 (absolute units) for A+/A- cells

Using A+/A- in a stream whose Likelihood has no asym= is an error; there is no silent default. Either add ; asym=<number>, or use the explicit A->B form, which carries its own deviation.

Under-reporting and coverage models

When “observed < true” comes from a mechanism, say you see only a fraction of cases (a reporting rate, a cohort coverage), model it directly rather than as a bound. The Formula column already refers to parameters by name, so give the stream a coverage factor:

Formula       Parameters
rho*X2        rho=Beta(2,2)     # reported = rho * true infected; rho fitted

rho can be fixed (*rho=0.7) or fitted with any prior. This gets you more than a bound does, but rho trades off with the epidemic scale, so it needs an anchor: a second, fully observed stream, a fixed population N0, or an informative prior on rho. This is a modelling pattern, not a cell type.

dataDummy: derived series

These are extra series to evaluate on the trajectory and overlay on plots, handy for looking at combinations of compartments (prevalence X2/(X1+X2+X3), say, or a subpopulation sum). Each row is just a Label and a Formula (the Label again defaults to the Formula). Dummy series carry no likelihood and are never fitted.

Simulate without fitting

If every state and parameter in the sheet is fixed (*name=val), there is nothing to estimate. You can run the model forward with no dataCombined at all and evaluate the dummy formulas on the trajectory:

sim <- simulate_model(sc$modelParams, data_dummy = sc$dataDummy,
                      solver = solver_control(backend = "r"))
sim                          # compartments, time span, fixed parameter values
head(sim$sir_out)            # the solved trajectory
plot_simulation(sim)$grid    # one panel per compartment / evaluated series

If any quantity is still fittable, simulate_model() says so and points you at fitCompartmentalModel(). Fixed-value *_sim example scenarios (SIR_sim, SEIR_sim, and so on) ship with the package.

Fit by maximum likelihood 

fit <- fitCompartmentalModel(
  modelParams  = sc$modelParams,
  dataCombined = sc$dataCombined,
  method       = "lbfgsb",                      # or "deoptim" (global), "hypercube"
  control      = optim_control(maxit = 1000),   # progress = FALSE for a silent fit
  solver       = solver_control()               # backend = "r" for a Julia-free fit
)

summary(fit)
get_point(fit)        # named point estimate (initial states plus parameters)

method = "lbfgsb" is a fast deterministic local search. "deoptim" is a stochastic global search (differential evolution), more robust on rugged objectives but slower. "hypercube" is a deterministic Sobol pre-scan. The *_control() helpers bundle the settings for each stage; see ?optim_control, ?hypercube_control, and ?solver_control.

Fit by Bayesian sampling

Pass method = "bayes" and a bayes_control() spec, and choose the sampler with the solver backend ("julia", "stan", or "r").

fit_b <- fitCompartmentalModel(
  modelParams  = sc$modelParams,
  dataCombined = sc$dataCombined,
  method       = "bayes",
  solver       = solver_control(),                        # or backend = "stan" / "r"
  bayes        = bayes_control(chains = 4, iter = 2000, warmup = 1000)
)

bayes_control(progress = FALSE) silences the sampler’s progress output on any backend. Inspect the posterior and its convergence:

posterior_report(fit_b)        # convergence verdict plus means and intervals
posterior_means(fit_b)
posterior_intervals(fit_b, p = 0.95)
plot_prior_posterior(fit_b)    # prior vs posterior, per parameter
identifiability_report(fit_b)  # narrowing, coverage, correlation diagnostics

A useful check is to compare the posterior against an MLE fit of the same model:

fit_mle <- fitCompartmentalModel(sc$modelParams, sc$dataCombined, "lbfgsb")
compare_to_mle(fit_b, fit_mle) # posterior mean and median vs MLE

Plot

plot_fit() returns per-stream plots, an arranged grid (if patchwork is installed), and the editable plotting code. Overlay dummy series with data_dummy.

res <- plot_fit(fit_b, data_dummy = sc$dataDummy, band_type = "both")
save_grid(res, sc$plot_path)   # writes a new numbered file; never overwrites

band_type sets the uncertainty display for Bayesian fits: "predictive", "mean", "both", or "spaghetti".

Colour scheme. Plots use the colour-blind-safe Okabe-Ito palette by default. For print or monochrome output pass palette = "grey" (or "grayscale"), or a custom palette list (see ?cfit_palette):

res_bw <- plot_fit(fit_b, palette = "grey")

To switch every plot at once, set the global option; a per-call palette still overrides it:

options(compfit.palette = "grey")   # back to colour: options(compfit.palette = "okabe")

Save and reload 

save_fit(fit_b, "Saved fits/fit.rds")
fit_b <- reload_fit("Saved fits/fit.rds")   # re-registers the backend and rebuilds the loss

Use reload_fit(path, register = FALSE) for a results-only read (posterior draws, no backend session).

Sensitivity

Global (variance-based, Sobol) sensitivity of the model outputs, summarised:

sob <- sobol_streams(fit_b, n = 500)
sobol_report(sob)              # validity, per-stream ranking, interactions, heatmap

Local (derivative) sensitivity at the fitted point:

ls <- local_sensitivity(fit_b, type = "relative")
plot_local_sensitivity(ls, kind = "tornado")

Reproducible export

extract_code() writes self-contained R source that reproduces the model, loss, and/or fit from a fit object, handy for sharing or archiving an analysis:

extract_code(fit_b, file = "reproduce.R", what = "all")
